note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before terminating 20 control cables in a marshalling panel, which documents should you have and check?
options: The supplier's latest price list for cables
A photo of another panel the firm has built
The cable schedule and wiring diagrams
The team's phone numbers and working hours

questions.stem: A new armoured cable must be connected into an existing panel that has other circuits in it. What is the right approach?
options: Work beside the live parts using insulated tools
Isolate the whole panel, lock, tag and prove dead
Switch off only the new circuit's breaker and start
Ask a co-worker to watch while you work

questions.stem: The armour of a steel-wire armoured (SWA) cable is to be used as the circuit's protective (earth) conductor. What must be confirmed?
options: That the armour wires are painted against rust
That the sheath is black, for sunlight
That the gland is plastic, for insulation
That the armour is big enough and well bonded

questions.stem: Which gland should be chosen for an SWA cable entering an outdoor panel that gets rain?
options: A gland with inner and outer seals, and a shroud
An indoor gland, which has no outer seal of any kind
A rubber grommet pushed into a hole cut to size
A nylon cable tie pulled around the cable

questions.stem: A large aluminium cable is to be connected to a copper busbar. What is needed?
options: A plain copper lug, crimped on with ordinary pliers
Solder poured onto the aluminium strands
A bimetal lug and the maker's jointing compound
Tape wrapped round the conductor and bar

questions.stem: When crimping a 95 mm² lug with a hydraulic tool, how do you choose the die?
options: Any die that happens to fit in the tool
The die the lug maker's table gives
The smallest die, for the tightest crimp
Whichever die was used on the last job

questions.stem: Which is a sign of a good crimp on a large lug?
options: Even die marks, no cracks, conductor fully in
A split barrel, with the strands showing through it
Conductor ending short inside the barrel
Lug turning freely around the conductor

questions.stem: After an MI cable end has been sealed, when is its insulation resistance usually checked again to confirm the seal is dry?
options: Never; one reading is enough for MI
Before the end is stripped, and not again
Again after a set time, as the maker advises
Only once the circuit has been switched on and loaded

questions.stem: Why are fire-resistant cables for fire alarm circuits fixed with metal clips rather than plastic ones?
options: Metal clips cost less than plastic ones
Plastic clips look untidy on walls
Metal clips grip the cable more tightly
Plastic clips would melt and let it fall

questions.stem: Why must an SWA cable not be bent tighter than its minimum bending radius where it enters a panel?
options: It makes the gland too hard to tighten
It changes the colour of the copper
It stretches the cable to a longer length
It can crack the insulation and bedding

questions.stem: As a common rule of thumb, the smallest bend radius for an unscreened Cat 6 cable is about how many times its outside diameter?
options: 1 times
2 times
4 times
20 times

questions.stem: Why must a data cable not be pulled too hard through a conduit?
options: It untwists the pairs and spoils performance
It makes the jacket fade and change colour
It only shortens the cable's paper warranty period
It makes the cable heavier to carry

questions.stem: In structured cabling, the fixed permanent link is usually limited to 90 m. Why is it less than the 100 m channel?
options: To save money on the cost of cable
To leave about 10 m for the patch leads
Because walls add to the cable length
Because data travels slower in walls

questions.stem: Which instrument checks a data link's wire map, length, crosstalk and loss, and gives a pass or fail against a category?
options: A plain continuity buzzer
A cable certification tester
An insulation resistance tester
A clamp meter on the cable

questions.stem: A Cat 6 link passes a simple wire-map test but fails certification for crosstalk. What is a likely cause?
options: The cable run is too short for the test
The patch panel is the wrong colour
The outlet faceplate screw is loose
Pairs untwisted too far at a termination

questions.stem: A screened (shielded) data cable is used in a factory. How should its screen be treated at the terminations?
options: Bonded via screened connectors to the earthed rack
Cut off at both ends and thrown away
Twisted together with one of the spare data pairs at each end
Folded back and taped to the outer jacket

questions.stem: Which fibre type is usually chosen for a link several kilometres long between buildings on a large site?
options: Multimode
Coax
Single-mode
Cat 6

questions.stem: Why must the end face of a fibre connector be inspected and cleaned before it is plugged in?
options: To make the ferrule shine for photos
Dirt can block light and scratch the face
To remove the colour code from the ferrule
So that it slides in more loosely

questions.stem: What is fusion splicing?
options: Joining two fibres with glue inside a small sleeve
Twisting two fibres tightly together
Holding fibres together with tape
Welding two fibre ends with an electric arc

questions.stem: A fibre link has 2 km of fibre at 0.4 dB per km, two connector pairs at 0.5 dB each and one splice at 0.1 dB. What is its expected total loss?
options: 1.9 dB
1.0 dB
2.4 dB
0.9 dB

questions.stem: Which instrument sends light pulses down a fibre and shows the distance to splices, connectors and breaks?
options: A digital multimeter
A copper cable certifier
An optical time-domain reflectometer
A clamp-on current meter

questions.stem: Why should you never look through a fibre inspection microscope at a fibre that may be connected to working equipment?
options: Invisible laser light could be focused into your eye
The microscope's lens would press on the ferrule and break it
It would slow down the network for users
Warm breath would fog up the microscope lens

questions.stem: When choosing coax for a long run to a satellite dish, what does the maker's attenuation figure (dB per 100 m) tell you?
options: How heavy the cable is per 100 m
The price of each 100 m of cable
How much signal is lost along the run
How many colours the jacket comes in

questions.stem: A 4–20 mA instrument signal is noisy at the controller. The cable screen is earthed at both ends, at different earth points. What is the likely fix?
options: Remove the screen from the cable entirely
Earth the screen at one end, as drawn
Add a third earth halfway along the run
Raise the loop current above 20 mA

questions.stem: A thermocouple must be extended from a furnace to its controller. Which cable should be used?
options: Ordinary copper twin-and-earth cable
Coaxial cable that was left over from a satellite TV job
Cat 6 data cable with two pairs used
Extension cable matched to the thermocouple type

questions.stem: Which is the right way to shrink a heat-shrink sleeve on a cable termination?
options: Hold a naked flame close to one side
Heat evenly with a heat gun, as the maker says
Heat one spot until the sleeve smokes
Use a cigarette lighter for the small sleeves on site

questions.stem: On a medium-voltage cable termination, why is a stress-control tube or tape fitted where the cable's semiconducting screen ends?
options: To make the end waterproof and nothing else
To spread electric stress at the screen end
To hold the lug firmly onto the conductor
To show which phase the core belongs to

questions.stem: Why should a crimped ferrule's size match the conductor's cross-section, rather than just being one that fits over it?
options: Because ferrule colours are only there for decoration
A smaller one always looks neater
An oversized one crimps loosely on the strands
A larger ferrule carries far more current

questions.stem: Why should both ends of every specialist cable carry the same unique label from the cable schedule?
options: So each cable can be traced end to end
So the installation looks smart to the client
So the client can be charged for more labels
So the jacket colour can be checked later

questions.stem: A new screened control cable is connected to a PLC input card at one end. What should you do before an insulation resistance test on the cable?
options: Test with the card left connected
Use the highest test voltage on the tester
Test only one core and assume the rest
Disconnect the cores from the card first

questions.stem: An insulation test between the cores of a new 50 m SWA cable reads 0.3 MΩ, while similar cables on the job read over 200 MΩ. What should you do?
options: Accept it, since any reading above zero counts as a pass
Find the cause, such as damage or damp, first
Raise the test voltage until the reading goes up
Connect it, and test it again after a week in use

questions.stem: With the cable isolated, how do you check that the armour of an SWA cable is continuous from gland to gland?
options: By looking closely along the outer sheath
With a two-pole voltage tester
With a low-resistance ohmmeter, tag to tag
By giving the cable a firm pull at each end

questions.stem: When terminating a three-phase SWA cable between a board and a motor, how should the cores be matched?
options: Same core to the same phase at both ends
Any core to any phase; it does not matter
By the colour of the gland at each end
By which core happens to be the longest

questions.stem: A cable is needed for a hot oven element. What should be checked first?
options: The colour of its outer sheath
Its price per metre at the store
Its temperature rating against the heat
Its length, and nothing else

questions.stem: A fire-resistant cable for an alarm sounder enters a metal box. Which gland should be used?
options: Any plastic gland from the store
The gland its cable maker specifies
A rubber grommet pushed into the hole
No gland, so the cable can move freely

questions.stem: How should the bolt holding a cable lug to a busbar be tightened?
options: To the maker's torque, then marked as checked
As tight as possible, using a long bar on the spanner
Hand-tight only, so it can be undone
Until the lug starts to bend upwards

questions.stem: Why do some electricians draw a paint line across a torqued nut and the busbar?
options: To show which size spanner it takes
To make the board look tidy
To show which phase it belongs to
So later loosening shows at a glance

questions.stem: A crimp lug is found discoloured, and the cable insulation near it is brittle. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cable run was much longer than it needed to be
The lug was the wrong colour for the phase
A poor crimp or loose bolt made it overheat
The lug surface was cleaned too well

questions.stem: A cable is to be jointed underground. Which method should be used?
options: A joint kit made for that cable's type and size
Several layers of PVC insulating tape
A plastic bag tied around the joint
An indoor junction box, buried directly in the soil

questions.stem: A cable jointing resin must be mixed on site. What should you read first?
options: The price label on the box
The pictures on the box
The label on the cable drum
The kit instructions and the SDS

questions.stem: When terminating Cat 6 cables onto a patch panel, which wiring scheme must be followed?
options: Any order, as long as it looks neat
The one scheme chosen for the whole site
A different colour order in each room
The reverse order at each end of the link

questions.stem: Why are compression connectors usually preferred to twist-on connectors on outdoor coax?
options: They seal and grip better
They always cost less
They need no tools to fit
They lower the cable's impedance

questions.stem: After terminating and testing specialist cables, what should be handed to the client?
options: Only the invoice for the work
A box of the cable off-cuts
Cable schedules and test results
A list of the tools the team used

questions.stem: A trainee on your team strips SWA armour by sawing deep into the bedding all the way round. What should you do?
options: Leave him to learn from his own mistakes this time
Finish the job yourself and say nothing
Report him to the manager straight away
Stop him, show him, and check his next one

questions.stem: Why is a little extra length coiled and left at each end of a data cable run?
options: To use up the rest of the drum
So it can be re-terminated later
To add weight so it hangs straight
To make the data signal stronger

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters OTDR stand for?
What is the name of the tool that cuts a glass fibre end cleanly and squarely before it is spliced?
In what unit is the light loss in a fibre link given?
What do the letters LSZH (sometimes written LS0H) stand for on a cable that gives off little smoke and no halogen gas in a fire?
What kind of lug is used to connect an aluminium conductor to a copper terminal?
What is the name of the method that joins two glass fibre ends permanently by melting them with an electric arc?
In a 4–20 mA instrument loop, what current in mA usually stands for the bottom of the measuring range?
What do the letters CPC stand for?
Which category of twisted-pair cable (5e, 6 or 6A) supports 10 gigabit Ethernet over the full 100 m channel?
A fibre link's loss budget is 3.0 dB and its measured loss is 2.2 dB. How much margin is left, in dB?
What type of gland seals each core in a setting compound where a cable enters equipment in an area with explosive gas?
What is the name of the layer around the insulation of a medium-voltage cable that controls the electric field and is earthed?
Which small push-pull fibre connector, with a 1.25 mm ferrule, is the most common in network racks?
What do the letters PoE stand for, when a data cable also carries power to a camera or wireless access point?
An armoured cable's insulation reading falls after it has lain in a flooded trench with a damaged end. What has most likely got into it?

essays.stem: Your team must terminate 16 power, control and instrument cables in a new marshalling panel at a water treatment plant. Explain how you would plan the work before the first cable is stripped.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first get the latest drawings, wiring diagrams and the cable schedule, which lists each cable's number, type, size, route and where each core lands. I check the cables delivered match the schedule and check their condition. I plan the order of work and the layout in the panel: power cables enter in one area and instrument cables in another, keeping them apart to avoid interference. I check that the right glands, lugs, ferrules, markers and screen-earthing parts are on site for each cable type, and that the crimp tools have the right dies and the torque tools are set. I plan the safe isolation of any supply to the panel with locks and tags, and proving dead. I share out the work by skill, with a checker for each cable, and prepare an inspection checklist and test sheets for continuity and insulation resistance. Finally, I brief the team on the schedule, the safety rules and how to record their work.
markingPoints: Gets current drawings, wiring diagrams and cable schedule
Checks delivered cables and materials against the schedule
Plans layout and segregation of power and instrument cables
Checks tools, dies and torque settings; plans safe isolation
Shares work, sets inspection and test records, briefs the team

essays.stem: Describe how to terminate a 4-core 95 mm² SWA cable onto the busbars of a switchboard, from preparing the cable to the final checks.
essays.modelAnswer: The switchboard is isolated, locked off and tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked before and after. I check the cable route and that the bend at the entry is not tighter than the maker's minimum radius. I fit the gland's shroud and outer parts, measure and mark the cable, then remove the outer sheath without cutting the armour. I cut the armour wires to length without nicking the bedding, fit them between the gland cone and clamping ring, and fit the earth tag, then tighten the gland so it seals and grips. I strip the bedding, cut each core to length for its phase position, and remove the insulation to the lug depth. I choose lugs for 95 mm² and the stud size, crimp them with a hydraulic tool and the matching die, and inspect each crimp. I bolt each lug to the right phase, matching the other end, and tighten to the maker's torque, marking each bolt. Finally, I test armour continuity, core continuity and insulation resistance, and record the results.
markingPoints: Safe isolation of the board: off, lock, tag, prove dead with checked tester
Prepares cable: bend radius, sheath and armour cut without damaging bedding
Fits gland correctly with armour clamped and earth tag fitted
Correct lugs crimped with matching die, inspected, connected to right phases
Torque to maker's value, marked; continuity and insulation tests recorded

essays.stem: Explain how a fibre link between two buildings should be terminated and tested, and the safety precautions the team must take.
essays.modelAnswer: The fibre is terminated in a patch panel at each end, either by fusion splicing factory-made pigtails onto the fibres or by fitting connectors, as the design says. Each fibre is stripped, cleaned and cleaved with the proper tools, spliced and protected in a splice tray, and labelled. Before any connector is mated, its end face is inspected with a scope and cleaned if needed. The link is tested with a light source and power meter, and the loss is compared with the loss budget, worked out from the fibre length and the number of connectors and splices. An OTDR may be used to show where any loss happens. Results are recorded for each fibre. For safety, nobody looks into a fibre or connector that may carry laser light, and inspection scopes are used only on fibres known to be disconnected. Fibre off-cuts are like glass needles, so they go into a marked, sealed container, and the team wears safety glasses, works on a dark mat and does not eat or drink at the bench.
markingPoints: Terminates by fusion splicing pigtails or fitting connectors; strip, clean, cleave, protect, label
Inspects and cleans end faces before mating
Tests with light source and power meter against a loss budget (OTDR as needed) and records
Never looks into a live fibre; scopes only on disconnected fibres
Off-cuts in a sealed container, glasses worn, no eating at the bench

essays.stem: Describe good practice when installing and terminating Cat 6A data cables in an office, so that every link will pass certification.
essays.modelAnswer: The cables are kept apart from power cables, as the design says, and away from sources of interference such as fluorescent ballasts and motors. They are not pulled harder than the maker allows, and not bent tighter than the minimum bend radius, so the pairs keep their twist. They are supported in trays, hooks or trunking, without tight cable ties that crush the jacket. At each end, a short service loop is left. When terminating, the sheath is removed only as far as needed and the pairs are untwisted as little as possible. The same wiring scheme (T568A or T568B) is used at both ends and across the whole site. Each cable is labelled at both ends to match the schedule. Termination is done with the right punch-down tool or the connector maker's tool. Finally, each link is tested with a certifier, and the results are saved and handed over.
markingPoints: Segregation from power and interference
Pulling tension and bend radius kept within limits; proper support without crushing
Minimal sheath removal and untwisting at terminations
Same wiring scheme throughout; labelled both ends; service loops
Each link certified and results saved

essays.stem: Explain why aluminium conductors need special care when they are terminated, and describe how to make a reliable termination.
essays.modelAnswer: Aluminium forms a hard oxide skin on its surface very quickly, which has a high resistance. Aluminium is also softer than copper and can creep away from a bolted joint over time, so the joint can loosen. Where aluminium touches copper with moisture present, corrosion can occur between the two metals. All of these can make a joint run hot and fail. To make a reliable termination, I use lugs or connectors made for aluminium, or bimetal lugs where the cable joins a copper terminal. I clean the strands with a wire brush to break the oxide, and apply the maker's jointing compound straight away to keep air and moisture out. I crimp the lug with the correct tool and die, then bolt it with the right washers and tighten to the maker's torque, and mark it. On larger joints, the torque is re-checked later as the maker advises. I record the work so it can be inspected.
markingPoints: Explains the oxide layer and its high resistance
Explains creep or loosening, and corrosion with copper
Uses aluminium-rated or bimetal lugs
Cleans the strands and applies jointing compound
Correct crimp, torque, marking and re-checking as advised

essays.stem: Explain how fire-resistant cables for a fire alarm system should be installed and terminated, and how the circuits should be tested.
essays.modelAnswer: The cable must be of the fire-resistant type named in the design. It is supported with metal clips or ties, not plastic ones, so it stays in place in a fire instead of falling and breaking. It is kept apart from other circuits or separated as the design requires, and is clearly identified, often with a red sheath. Where it enters boxes, the glands named by the cable maker are used, and the ends are prepared as the maker says, without damaging the fire-resistant layer. Terminations are made in the devices' terminals, tightened to the right torque. Holes through fire walls are sealed with fire-stopping. For testing, the system is isolated, and the detectors, sounders and the control panel are disconnected so they are not damaged. Then continuity and insulation resistance tests are carried out on each circuit and recorded. Function testing of the whole system is done later by the fire alarm specialist.
markingPoints: Correct fire-resistant cable, supported with metal fixings
Segregated and identified
Maker's glands and termination method, correct torque, fire-stopping at walls
Devices and panel disconnected before insulation tests
Continuity and insulation tests recorded; system function test by specialist

essays.stem: Describe the main parts of a heat-shrink termination kit for a medium-voltage cable and what each does, and explain why only trained, authorised people may make such terminations.
essays.modelAnswer: A medium-voltage cable has a conductor, insulation, a semiconducting screen and a metallic screen, then a sheath. Where the cable is terminated, the screens must be cut back, and this concentrates the electric stress at the screen edge. The kit has a stress-control tube or mastic that spreads this stress so the insulation does not break down. It has an outer heat-shrink insulating tube to protect the exposed insulation from moisture and tracking, and sheds on outdoor terminations to give a longer path over the surface. It has an earthing connection for the metallic screen, sealing mastic, and the lug. The cutting distances in the kit's instructions are critical: a small error or a scratch in the insulation can cause a failure or an explosion when energised. That is why only people trained and authorised for medium voltage may do this work, with the cable isolated, earthed and proved dead under the power company's or site's permit system.
markingPoints: Stress-control tube or mastic spreads the stress at the screen end
Insulating tube and sheds protect against moisture and surface tracking
Screen earthing, sealing and lug parts named
Exact dimensions and clean, undamaged insulation are critical
Only trained, authorised people; cable isolated, earthed and under a permit

essays.stem: A 4–20 mA level signal from a tank to a control panel is unsteady. Explain how cable selection, routing, screening and terminations can cause or cure this kind of problem.
essays.modelAnswer: Instrument signals are small, so they can easily pick up electrical noise. The cable should be a screened twisted pair, because twisting cancels much of the noise and the screen stops interference from outside. If the cable runs alongside power cables or motor drive cables, noise is induced into it, so it should be routed apart from them, as the design says, and cross power cables at right angles. The screen should usually be earthed at one end only, often at the panel end, because earthing both ends at different earth points can let current flow in the screen and cause noise. At the terminations, the screen and its drain wire should be sleeved so they do not touch other terminals or the enclosure, and the cores should be terminated firmly with ferrules. Loose or corroded terminals add resistance and can cause the reading to jump. Checking each of these, with the circuit isolated, usually finds the cause.
markingPoints: Uses screened twisted pair and explains why
Routes away from power and drive cables; crosses at right angles
Screen earthed at one end, explaining earth loops
Screen and drain sleeved; firm terminations with ferrules
Loose or corroded terminals cause unsteady readings; checked with circuit isolated

essays.stem: As the Level 3 member leading a group of trainees terminating specialist cables, explain how you would make sure the quality of every termination is right.
essays.modelAnswer: Before work starts, I brief the group on the cable schedule, the safety rules and the standard for each type of termination, and show a good example of each. I check that every member has the right tools, dies and torque settings, and that glands, lugs and ferrules match the cables. I set hold points where work must be checked before it continues: for example after the armour is clamped in the gland, after lugs are crimped, and before an enclosure is closed. At each hold point I or a second member inspect the work against a checklist, such as no damaged insulation, correct crimp, no bare conductor showing, correct torque and labels on both ends. I give feedback straight away and have faults put right. All tests are done and recorded, and anything that fails is reworked and retested. Finally, I sign the inspection records and note any training needs for members who struggled.
markingPoints: Briefs on schedule, safety and the standard, with an example
Checks tools, dies, torque settings and materials
Sets hold points with checklist inspections
Gives feedback and has faults corrected; tests recorded and failures reworked
Signs records and notes training needs

essays.stem: After installation, two of twelve Cat 6 links in a school computer lab fail certification. Explain how you would find and correct the causes.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first look at the certifier's results for the two failed links to see which test failed and where. A wire-map fault, such as a crossed or split pair or an open conductor, points to a termination error. A length failure means the run is too long and may need re-routing or a switch nearer the room. Crosstalk failures (NEXT) usually come from too much untwisting at a termination, and the tester often shows which end. Insertion-loss failures may come from a damaged, kinked or crushed cable or a poor-quality patch lead. I would inspect the outlets and patch panel terminations at the end shown, and look along the route for crushed cable ties, tight bends or cable near power cables or lights. I would re-terminate the faulty end with the pairs untwisted as little as possible, or replace damaged cable, then re-certify. The new passing results are saved with the others and handed over, and I note the cause so the team avoids it in future.
markingPoints: Reads which test failed and where from the certifier
Links wire-map faults to termination errors and length failures to route length
Links crosstalk to untwisting and loss to damaged cable or poor leads
Inspects terminations and route; re-terminates or replaces
Re-certifies, saves results and records the cause for the team

practical1.title: Plan, terminate and test SWA power cables and a screened instrument cable into a marshalling enclosure, with schedule and records
practical1.brief: As a group, terminate two SWA power cables and one screened multicore instrument cable between a marshalling enclosure and two field enclosures on the training board, working from the drawing given by the assessor. First, write a termination schedule for every core (cable number, core, terminal, label) and agree a layout that keeps power and instrument cables apart. The board is isolated, every member fits their own lock and tag, and it is proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Share the work so that every member terminates at least one cable end: glands with the armour clamped and earth tags fitted, crimped lugs or ferrules, core markers to the schedule, the instrument screen and drain wire sleeved and earthed at the marshalling end only, and terminals tightened to the stated torque. At two hold points (glands done; cores terminated) another member inspects the work against the checklist and initials it. Then carry out and record armour continuity, core continuity and insulation resistance tests at 500 V DC. Hand in the completed schedule as an as-built record. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training board with a marshalling enclosure, two field enclosures, terminal rails and an earth bar
Two lengths of multicore SWA cable and one length of screened multicore instrument cable, about 1.5 m each
Outdoor-type glands to suit the SWA, with earth tags, locknuts and shrouds; a gland for the instrument cable
Lugs or ferrules, crimp tools with matching dies, core markers, heat-shrink or sleeving for the drain wire
Cable knife, armour cutting saw, strippers, spanners and a torque screwdriver
Lock, tag, multi-lock hasp, voltage tester and proving unit
Low-resistance ohmmeter and insulation resistance tester
Drawing from the assessor, blank termination schedule, inspection checklist and test sheet
photos: The completed termination schedule and the agreed panel layout
The board isolated with every member's lock, and the tester on the proving unit
An SWA gland fitted, with the armour clamped and the earth tag in place
The instrument cable end, with the screen and drain wire sleeved and earthed at one end
The finished marshalling enclosure, with every core marked
The initialled inspection checklist and the completed test sheet
checklist: Helped write a complete, accurate termination schedule
Took part in safe isolation and kept the board dead
Terminated their cable end neatly: gland correct, armour clamped, no damage to bedding or insulation
Crimped lugs or ferrules with the right tool and die; no bare conductor showing
Marked every core to the schedule and tightened terminals to the stated torque
Inspected another member's work at a hold point and recorded the result
Carried out and recorded continuity and insulation tests correctly
safety: The board stays isolated, locked and tagged; prove dead with a tester checked before and after
Cut armour away from the body and wear cut-resistant gloves; armour ends are sharp
Warn others before insulation tests and keep hands off the conductors during them
Put armour and sheath off-cuts in the scrap bin straight away

practical2.title: Install, terminate and test a small structured cabling system and a CCTV coax run, with a test report
practical2.brief: As a group, install and terminate four Cat 6 permanent links from a small patch panel to four outlets on the training wall, and one coax run with compression connectors from a camera position to a recorder position. Plan first: choose and agree one wiring scheme (T568A or T568B) for the whole job, number each link, and draw a simple labelled layout. Every member installs and terminates at least one link, keeping within the bend radius, leaving a service loop, untwisting the pairs as little as possible, and labelling both ends. One member terminates the coax with compression connectors. Then test each link with the cable certifier (or, if the Centre has none, a wire-map and length tester), save or photograph each result, find and correct any failure, and retest. If the Centre has fibre equipment, the assessor may add one fibre patch link to be inspected, cleaned and tested with a light source and power meter. The group writes a short test report with a results table and the labelled layout. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Cat 6 cable, a small patch panel and four outlets with back boxes or surface boxes
Punch-down tool, sheath stripper, side cutters and cable supports
Coax cable, compression connectors, coax stripping tool and compression tool
Cable certifier, or a wire-map and length tester
Labels and a label printer or marker
Optional, as the Centre has them: fibre patch leads, inspection scope, cleaning kit, light source and power meter
Blank layout sheet and test report form
photos: The labelled layout showing the chosen wiring scheme
Cables installed with supports, bend radius kept and service loops left
A finished patch panel termination, close up, showing little untwisting
A finished outlet and its label
A tester screen showing a pass result for each link
